turn_text: Coming out of committee you had five votes against the bill coming from southern senators who represented peanuts cotton and rice. Is there any room in the bill to offer anything to those southern interests to keep it on track?

Well, you know, there is a lot of work that needs to be done with them, and I think that there's always a chance of getting a compromise on peanuts and rice. That's the hope, and I know people are continuing to work that not only in the Senate side, my colleague from Minnesota, Colin Peterson, is also working on that. And traditionally, people have come together across party lines and geographic lines for the farm bill, so we'll continue to work on that.
Are there any amendments coming forth to this farm bill that you know of?

Well, there will be a number of amendments to try to shift some of the funding. From my perspective, we have already cut 23 billion, which we needed to do given our debt situation. But 16 billion or about two thirds of the cuts are from the farm programs. And in fact, the farm programs are only 14% of the bill. And I think people don't always know that. And one of the reasons we were able to get such a strong vote is that we're able to keep the support of conservation groups. 640 conservation groups are supporting this bill, as well as the nutrition groups with the school lunch program and other things. But I think people need to remember us. They will clearly put an amendment to shift things and to get rid of parts of the bill. They have to remember that the bulk of the cuts nearly two-thirds of them came on the farm end to the 14 percent of the bill that the farm program.

turn_text: You have an election later this year as does Senator Stabenow. Is there need for this bill to be finished before the election to put you in the best light?

You know, I don't think there's anything much to do with an election cycle as much as it has to do with the cycle of the farm bill. That farm bill has to be reauthorized because if we don't have a new farm bill, we literally are going to go into next year. No one knows what will happen. because of the fact that we always have a farm bill in place. One of the best things about the economy in a very challenging time has been rural America. When you look at Minnesota, we're down to 5.6% unemployment. A lot of that has to do with our ag economy and how that feeds into companies like General Mills and Land of Lakes and Hormol and others. We are well aware of the fact that's important for our economy, for the rural areas, and that's what brings us to this timing, not the election cycle. The only way the election cycle plays in as far as I'm concerned is that it gets harder and harder to do stuff as it gets closer to the election, so it would be much better to get this done this summer and get the Senate bill done in the next week or two and then move it right over to the House so that they can get something done and then we could get a conference committee done before August.

turn_text: Ms. Klobuchar, would you comment on your view on U.S. trade negotiations, especially the pending one for the Trans-Pacific Partnership?

Well, I have been supportive of some of the trade deals and not all of them, but I basically think there were some really important ones that came up recently. I was very supportive of the Korean deal just because you could see the potential for AG. We've had something like a 20-some percent increase in AG exports in Minnesota in the last few years. It's an incredible story nationally and as long as we put some provisions in these trade agreements for workers' training and for also to make sure that there is fair as we can get, I think that which the administration worked very hard on this time. I think there's some real positives for our country. I think you saw some pretty broad support for the agreements this past time which some people were surprised by. So hopefully that will bode well for agreements going forward.
